podcast.body: This was the very first song Trent Reznor wrote in his new, harder, and more sinister style, moving beyond his techno-pop influences. The original version was about half the speed of the record version and was admitted by Trent to be "a total ripoff of Dig It, my Skinny Puppy." Lyrically, it stemmed from a train-of-thought process, reflecting Trent's coming-of-age realization that earlier illusions about life's certainties were false, leading to a feeling of things not working out as hoped. "That was the first song I'd ever written. When I sat down, I took a very experimental approach to it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Original Video Mistaken by FBI as Snuff Film
podcast.body: For the first NIN single from *Pretty Hate Machine*, Trent Reznor and directors Eric Zimmerman and Benjamin Stokes filmed a video in a Cleveland warehouse in September 1989. In the first draft, Trent appeared to fall from a building and die bloody in the street. A camera was attached to a helium weather balloon for aerial shots, but the rope snapped and the camera floated 200 miles away before landing in a farmer's field. The farmer took it to the police, who watched the footage and concluded it was a snuff film showing a real corpse decomposing. Forensic experts agreed the "body" had been there at least three weeks. The FBI was called. Eventually the situation was resolved; the original video was apparently never publicly released, and a new version was shot instead. "Forensic experts poured over the film and came to the conclusion that yes, it did show a real rotting corpse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: A song from Nine Inch Nails' first album. Its music video depicted Trent Reznor being chased through Chicago, pushed off a building, and lying in a pool of blood. Due to budget constraints, aerial shots were filmed by attaching a camera to a balloon, which subsequently detached and drifted 150 miles east to Burr Oak, Michigan. A farmer found the camera and gave it to police, who, misinterpreting the footage as an actual murder (thinking the body was genuine and rotting), launched an FBI investigation that lasted a year. The case was only solved when a university student, who had seen the video (without the death shot) on MTV and an FBI flyer, connected the dots. "The plot shows Trent being chased through the streets of Chicago by a couple of baddies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
